svg.text: Kangaroo mother care, and getting the attachment right
Kangaroo mother care
Baby upright between the breasts, skin to skin,
head turned to one side, airway clear
Hips flexed and abducted, frog position
Secured with a wrapper, cap on the head
Continuous, or as many hours as possible
It regulates temperature, breathing and heart
rate, improves feeding and reduces mortality
in low birth weight babies. The father can do it too.
Signs of good attachment — all four
Chin touching the breast
Mouth wide open
Lower lip turned outwards
More areola visible ABOVE than below
Effective suckling is slow and deep with pauses,
and you can hear or see the baby swallowing.
Sore, cracked nipples nearly always mean poor attachment.
Engorgement or mastitis — the answer is almost never to stop feeding
Engorgement: both breasts, tight, shiny, tender, usually day 3 to 5. Feed more often, express to soften the areola first.
Mastitis: one breast, a red wedge-shaped area, fever and flu-like aching. Continue feeding from that breast.
Milk must keep moving. Stopping feeds turns mastitis into an abscess.
Antibiotics if no improvement in 24 hours, if there is a nipple fissure, or if she is severely unwell.
Low birth weight, by the numbers
Low birth weight under 2,500 g · Very low under 1,500 g · Extremely low under 1,000 g
Preterm is before 37 completed weeks. Small for gestational age is below the tenth centile for the gestation.
A baby can be preterm, small for dates, or both — and the causes and the care differ, so do not use the terms loosely.
